stem: In the Next.js 16 App Router, where can you call `(await cookies()).set('session', token, {...})` to create a login session?

options.text: Inside any Server Component, as long as it is async
options.why: Server Components can read cookies but cannot set them during rendering.

options.text: Inside a Server Function (Server Action) or a Route Handler
options.why: Those run where a response header can still be written, so a Set-Cookie can be sent.

options.text: Inside a Client Component through the same next/headers import
options.why: next/headers is server-only; Client Components cannot import it.

options.text: Inside the root layout, so the cookie applies to every page
options.why: Layouts are Server Components too, and setting cookies during render is not supported.

explanation: The `cookies()` API reads incoming cookies in Server Components but can only write (`set`, `delete`) in Server Functions and Route Handlers. HTTP does not allow setting cookies after streaming starts, and rendering streams HTML, so Next.js blocks cookie writes during render. A login form should therefore submit to a Server Action that creates the session cookie and then redirects.
reference: Next.js docs: cookies() (Good to know)

stem: An environment variable named `NEXT_PUBLIC_STRIPE_KEY` is inlined into the JavaScript sent to the browser at `next build` time, so any value stored in it should be treated as public.

options.text: True
options.why: Next.js replaces references to NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables with their build-time values in client bundles.

options.text: False
options.why: The NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix is exactly the opt-in that exposes a value to the browser.

explanation: By default environment variables are only available on the server. Prefixing a name with `NEXT_PUBLIC_` tells Next.js to inline the value into the client bundle at build time, which means anyone can read it in the downloaded JavaScript. Only publishable values (such as a Stripe publishable key) belong there; secret keys must stay unprefixed and be read on the server. Inlined values are also frozen at build time, so changing them later requires a rebuild.
reference: Next.js docs: Environment Variables

stem: You store a signed session token in a cookie. Which three cookie options does the Next.js authentication guide recommend? (Choose three.)

options.text: `httpOnly: true`
options.why: It stops client-side JavaScript from reading the cookie, which limits damage from XSS.

options.text: `secure: true`
options.why: The cookie is only sent over HTTPS, so it cannot be read on the wire.

options.text: `sameSite: 'lax'`
options.why: SameSite limits when the browser sends the cookie on cross-site requests, which helps against CSRF.

options.text: Copying the token into localStorage as a backup
options.why: localStorage is readable by any script on the page, which defeats httpOnly.

options.text: Putting the user's email and phone number in the payload
options.why: The guide says the payload should hold minimal data such as the user ID and role, not personal data.

explanation: The guide recommends setting the session cookie on the server with HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, an expiry (Max-Age or Expires) and a Path. The payload should contain only the minimum needed to identify the user, such as the ID and role. Personally identifiable or sensitive data does not belong in a cookie, and tokens should never be mirrored into storage that scripts can read.
reference: Next.js docs: Authentication (Setting cookies)

stem: A teammate says: "Our `deleteAccount` Server Action is safe without an auth check, because the only button that calls it is on a page that already requires login." What is wrong with this reasoning?

options.text: Anyone can POST to the action directly, so it must check auth itself
options.why: Server Actions are reachable endpoints, independent of which page shows the button.

options.text: Nothing: actions inherit the auth check of the page that renders them
options.why: A page-level check only controls what UI renders; it does not run for the action request.

options.text: Only GET requests can bypass the page, and actions use GET
options.why: Server Actions use POST, and that does not make them private.

options.text: The page check is enough, but only if the action file is marked `server-only`
options.why: server-only prevents client imports; it does not authenticate callers.

explanation: Next.js documents that an exported Server Action is reachable via a direct POST request, not just through your UI. Treat every action like a public API endpoint: authenticate the caller, authorize the specific operation, and validate the input inside the action (or in a Data Access Layer it calls). Rendering the form only for logged-in users is a UX choice, not a security boundary.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (Mutating Data)

stem: A module in `lib/` reads the database and private API keys. Which package do you import at the top of it so that the build fails if any Client Component imports that module? Type the package name.
explanation: `import 'server-only'` marks a module as server-only. If it ends up in the client module graph, the build fails with an error instead of shipping server code to the browser. Next.js handles the import internally, so the npm package's contents are not even used. It complements a Data Access Layer: DAL modules import `server-only`, and only they touch `process.env` secrets and the database.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (Preventing client-side execution of server-only code)

stem: Match each authorization approach with how the Next.js authentication guide describes it.

options.text: Optimistic check
options.why: Reads the session from the cookie only.

options.text: Secure check
options.why: Uses session data stored in the database.

options.text: Data Access Layer (DAL)
options.why: Centralizes data requests and authorization.

options.text: Data Transfer Object (DTO)
options.why: Returns only the fields the caller needs.

explanation: The guide distinguishes optimistic checks, which read the session from the cookie and suit redirects and showing or hiding UI, from secure checks that consult the session data in the database before sensitive work. It recommends centralizing authorization in a Data Access Layer and returning minimal Data Transfer Objects, with Proxy as an optional place for optimistic redirects only.
reference: Next.js docs: Authentication (Authorization)

prompts.text: A Proxy reads the session cookie and redirects signed-out visitors before a page renders
Before a sensitive mutation, the server looks the session ID up in the sessions table
A server-only module whose `verifySession()` runs before every data request
A function that returns `{ id, name }` instead of the full user row

stem: A comment component renders user-submitted text. Which version is vulnerable to cross-site scripting (XSS)?

options.text:
`

{comment.body}

`
options.why: React escapes text children, so markup in the string is shown as text.

options.text:
`

`
options.why: Raw HTML is inserted without escaping, so injected script handlers run.

options.text:
`

Comment

`
options.why: React escapes attribute values, so a quote cannot break out of the attribute.

options.text:
`

{String(comment.body).trim()}

`
options.why: It is still a text child, which React escapes before rendering.

explanation: React escapes strings rendered as children or attribute values, so `` inside a comment appears as literal text. `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` bypasses that escaping on purpose. If you must render user HTML, sanitize it with an allowlist-based sanitizer first, and add a Content Security Policy as a second layer.
reference: react.dev: dangerouslySetInnerHTML

stem: A profile page renders `Website`, and an attacker sets their website to `javascript:alert(document.cookie)`. What does React 19 render for that link?

options.text: The `javascript:` URL unchanged, so clicking it runs the script
options.why: React 19 no longer passes javascript: URLs through to href.

options.text: A replacement `javascript:` URL that only throws an error
options.why: React 19 swaps it for a URL that throws "React has blocked a javascript: URL as a security precaution."

options.text: Nothing: the whole `<a>` element is dropped from the output
options.why: The element still renders; only the dangerous URL is replaced.

options.text: The URL with `javascript:` stripped, leaving `alert(document.cookie)`
options.why: React does not rewrite the URL into a relative link; it substitutes a blocked one.

explanation: Rendering `href="javascript:alert(1)"` with React 19 produces `href="javascript:throw new Error('React has blocked a javascript: URL as a security precaution.')"`, and the same applies to `src`. This protects links built from user data, but it is not a full defense. `router.push` with a `javascript:` URL still executes it, as the Next.js docs warn, and other schemes such as `data:` are not covered. Validate user URLs, for example allow only `https:`, before storing or rendering them.
reference: React 19 release notes; Next.js docs: useRouter (Good to know)

options.text: It should check `session.user.role === 'admin'` before deleting
options.why: Requiring admin would block normal users from deleting their own posts; ownership is the missing rule.

options.text: Any signed-in user can delete any post by sending a different `postId`
options.why: It checks authentication but never checks that the post belongs to the caller (IDOR).

options.text: `postId` must be read from FormData, because typed arguments are rejected
options.why: Actions can take typed arguments; how the ID arrives does not make it trustworthy.

options.text: It must call `revalidatePath` before deleting, or the delete is unsafe
options.why: Revalidation affects cached UI, not who is allowed to delete.

explanation: This is an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR). The action proves the caller is logged in (authentication) but not that they may act on this post (authorization). Because action arguments come from the client, an attacker can POST any ID. Load the resource and compare `post.authorId` with `session.user.id` (or call a `canDelete` policy) before deleting, ideally inside a server-only Data Access Layer.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (Authentication and authorization)

options.text: The redirect in the page runs first and blocks the request
options.why: The action is a separate POST entry point; the page body is not a guard for it.

options.text: The records are deleted, because the action never checks the caller
options.why: A page-level check does not extend to actions defined inside the page.

options.text: Next.js rejects it, because inline actions only accept calls from the same render
options.why: Inline actions are still callable endpoints; Next.js does not tie them to one render.

options.text: The CSRF Origin check blocks it, because the request was replayed
options.why: A same-origin replay from the user's own browser passes the Origin check.

explanation: Next.js documents exactly this case: the page-level redirect controls which UI renders, but the Server Action is its own entry point and must verify the caller itself. Add `const session = await auth(); if (!session?.user?.isAdmin) throw new Error('Unauthorized')` inside the action, or call a DAL function that does it. The Origin check only stops cross-site form posts; it does nothing against a logged-in user calling the action from your own origin.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (Authentication and authorization)

stem: A team protects `/dashboard/*` only with an auth check in `app/dashboard/layout.tsx`. Why does the Next.js authentication guide warn against relying on that? (Choose two.)

options.text: Layouts do not re-render on client navigation, so the check does not run on every route change
options.why: Partial rendering only renders the segments that change.

options.text: A layout does not control whether nested segments and parallel slots render
options.why: The router renders them anyway, so their output can still reach the RSC payload.

options.text: Layouts run only at build time, so they cannot read request cookies
options.why: Layouts can read cookies at request time; that is not the problem.

options.text: Layouts are Client Components, so any check in them is visible to users
options.why: Layouts are Server Components by default.

options.text: Calling redirect() in a layout is not supported in the App Router
options.why: redirect() works in layouts; the risk is coverage, not support.

explanation: Because of partial rendering, navigating between pages under the same layout re-renders only the changed segment, so a session check in the layout is not repeated. A layout that hides or swaps `{children}` or parallel slots also does not stop the router from rendering them. Put checks close to the data (the DAL) or in each page and leaf component that needs them.
reference: Next.js docs: Authentication (Layouts and auth checks)

options.text: Only `name`, because Next.js prunes props the component never reads
options.why: There is no pruning; React serializes the props as given.

options.text: Every column of the row, the password hash included
options.why: All props passed to a Client Component are serialized for the client.

options.text: Nothing, because Server Components never send data to the browser
options.why: Props to Client Components cross the boundary by design.

options.text: Only the columns that are strings, because other types are skipped
options.why: Serializable values of every supported type are sent.

explanation: Props passed from a Server Component to a Client Component are serialized into the RSC payload so the client can hydrate. React has no way to know which fields the component reads, so the whole object goes over the wire. The docs flag this exact pattern as EXPOSED. Return a minimal DTO such as `{ name }` from a data function, and keep Client Component prop types narrow so broad objects are rejected in review.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (Component-level data access)

stem: An `updateProfile` Server Action ends with `return db.user.update({ where: { id: session.user.id }, data })`. Why do the Next.js docs call this a bad pattern?

options.text: Returning a promise from an action makes the form submit twice
options.why: Returning a promise is normal; actions are async functions.

options.text: The full updated record is serialized and sent to the client
options.why: Action return values go to the browser, including internal fields.

options.text: The update runs before the auth check because returns are hoisted
options.why: JavaScript does not hoist return statements; the order is as written.

options.text: Actions must return FormData, so the record causes a runtime error
options.why: Actions can return any serializable value.

explanation: Whatever a Server Action returns is serialized and sent to the client, for example into `useActionState`. Returning the raw ORM result can leak columns such as password hashes, internal flags or tokens. Do the update, then return only what the UI needs, such as `{ success: true }` or a small DTO.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (Controlling return values)

stem: Put the steps of nonce-based Content Security Policy in a Next.js 16 app in the order they happen for one request.

options.text: Proxy generates a fresh random nonce for the request
options.why: Generation

options.text: Proxy sets a Content-Security-Policy containing that nonce on the request and the response
options.why: Propagation

options.text: During rendering, Next.js reads the nonce from the CSP header
options.why: Extraction

options.text: Next.js adds the nonce to framework scripts, page bundles and inline scripts it generates
options.why: Application

options.text: The browser runs only scripts whose nonce matches the policy
options.why: Enforcement

explanation: Proxy creates a unique nonce per request and sets it in the `Content-Security-Policy` header, optionally also in a custom `x-nonce` request header for your own code. During server rendering Next.js parses the CSP header, extracts the `'nonce-…'` value and attaches it automatically to its framework scripts, page bundles, the inline scripts it generates and any `<Script>` given the nonce. The browser then refuses scripts without a matching nonce.
reference: Next.js docs: Content Security Policy (How nonces work)

stem: An attacker's page embeds ``. Because the browser sends your cookies with that request, it can trigger a Server Action defined on the settings page.

options.text: True
options.why: An makes a GET request, and Server Actions only run for POST requests.

options.text: False
options.why: Server Actions only accept POST, so a GET from an image tag cannot invoke one.

explanation: Server Actions are invoked with POST, and only that method is allowed. Combined with SameSite cookies, this prevents most CSRF in modern browsers. As extra protection, Next.js compares the `Origin` header with the `Host` (or `X-Forwarded-Host`) and rejects mismatches. The docs also stress the flip side: never perform mutations during rendering, for example logging out when a query parameter is present, because a GET for that page would trigger it.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (Allowed origins; Avoiding side-effects during rendering)

stem:
A product page embeds structured data. A seller names their product `</script><script>alert(1)</script>`. What happens?

```tsx
<script
  type="application/ld+json"
  dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: JSON.stringify(jsonLd) }}
/>
```

options.text: Nothing: `JSON.stringify` escapes `<` and `>` in strings
options.why: JSON.stringify escapes quotes and backslashes, not angle brackets.

options.text: It closes the script tag early, so the injected script runs
options.why: The HTML parser ends the script element at the first `</script>`.

options.text: Nothing, because `type="application/ld+json"` is never executed
options.why: The JSON block is inert, but the injected second <script> is a normal script.

options.text: React escapes the content because it is inside a script tag
options.why: dangerouslySetInnerHTML inserts the string without escaping.

explanation: Rendering this with React 19 outputs the payload verbatim, so the HTML parser sees `</script>` and closes the element, then runs the attacker's `<script>`. The Next.js JSON-LD guide fixes it by escaping `<` before inserting: `JSON.stringify(jsonLd).replace(/</g, '\\u003c')`. The `\u003c` escape is still valid JSON for the same character but can no longer close the tag.
reference: Next.js docs: JSON-LD

stem: After login, a Client Component runs `router.push(searchParams.get('next') ?? '/')`. Why is this dangerous even though React 19 blocks `javascript:` URLs in `href`?

options.text: It is not dangerous: router.push only accepts paths inside the app
options.why: router.push accepts full URLs, including other schemes.

options.text: A `javascript:` URL passed to `router.push` executes in the page
options.why: The Next.js docs warn that router.push and router.replace run javascript: URLs.

options.text: It leaks the session cookie in the Referer header to the next page
options.why: Cookies are not sent in the Referer header.

options.text: It disables prefetching, which lets the attacker race the navigation
options.why: Prefetching has nothing to do with the injection.

explanation: React's `javascript:` protection applies to rendered attributes such as `href` and `src`. Programmatic navigation is different: the `useRouter` docs say `javascript:` URLs sent to `router.push` or `router.replace` are executed in the context of your page. Treat `next`, `callbackUrl` and similar parameters as untrusted. Accept only same-origin relative paths (and reject `//`), or map them to an allowlist.
reference: Next.js docs: useRouter (Good to know)

stem: A security scan flags that every response from your self-hosted Next.js app includes an `x-powered-by: Next.js` header, which advertises your framework. Which `next.config.js` option do you set to `false` to stop Next.js adding it? Type the option name.
explanation: By default Next.js adds an `x-powered-by` header. Setting `poweredByHeader: false` in `next.config.js` turns it off. Removing it does not fix any vulnerability, but it stops broadcasting the framework, which makes automated fingerprinting slightly harder. That is why many security baselines ask for it alongside proper headers such as a Content Security Policy.
reference: Next.js docs: poweredByHeader

stem: A `proxy.ts` lets a request through when `getSessionCookie(request)` returns a value, which only checks that a session cookie is present. Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: It is an optimistic check: an expired or revoked session still gets through
options.why: Presence of a cookie says nothing about whether the session is still valid.

options.text: Pages, Route Handlers and actions must still verify the session against the server
options.why: Real authorization belongs close to the data, as the docs recommend.

options.text: It is secure, because cookies cannot be created by the client
options.why: Anyone can send a request with any cookie header they like.

options.text: Proxy should instead query the database on every request
options.why: Proxy runs on every matched route, including prefetches, so the docs advise against DB checks there.

options.text: Proxy checks are pointless and should be removed
options.why: Optimistic redirects are useful for UX and for static routes; they just are not the only defense.

explanation: Checking only that a session cookie exists is fast but proves nothing about validity: the cookie may be expired, revoked or forged. The Next.js guide recommends exactly this split. Proxy does cookie-only optimistic checks and redirects, avoiding database work because it runs on every route and prefetch, while the Data Access Layer performs the secure check before any sensitive data is read or changed.
reference: Next.js docs: Authentication (Optimistic checks with Proxy)

stem: After adding nonce-based CSP in `proxy.ts`, the build output shows every page as dynamic, and your marketing pages are no longer served from the CDN cache. Why?

options.text: Proxy forces dynamic rendering for every route it matches
options.why: Proxy itself does not change how pages render.

options.text: Each nonce is per-request, so pages must render at request time
options.why: Static pages are generated at build time, when no request or nonce exists.

options.text: CSP headers cannot be cached by CDNs, so Next.js disables static output
options.why: Headers are cacheable; the problem is the per-request nonce inside the HTML.

options.text: The x-nonce header switches the app into development mode
options.why: It is an ordinary request header with no effect on build mode.

explanation: Next.js applies nonces during server-side rendering, based on the CSP header of the incoming request. A static page is generated at build time with no request, so no nonce can be injected, and a cached copy would replay one nonce to everyone. The docs therefore say nonce-based CSP requires dynamic rendering. Static optimization and ISR are disabled, CDN caching needs extra work, and Partial Prerendering is incompatible. If you need static pages with a strict CSP, the experimental Subresource Integrity (hash-based) approach is the documented alternative.
reference: Next.js docs: Content Security Policy (Static vs Dynamic Rendering)

stem: Your team is deciding whether to adopt nonce-based CSP across the whole app. Which three consequences are documented by Next.js? (Choose three.)

options.text: Pages must be dynamically rendered for every request
options.why: Each response needs a fresh nonce, which needs a request.

options.text: Static optimization and ISR stop applying to those pages
options.why: They depend on HTML generated ahead of requests.

options.text: Partial Prerendering (PPR) cannot be used with it
options.why: The prerendered static shell's scripts have no access to the nonce.

options.text: You must add `nonce={...}` by hand to every script Next.js emits
options.why: Next.js attaches the nonce to its own scripts automatically.

options.text: Development no longer needs `'unsafe-eval'` once a nonce is set
options.why: The docs say dev still needs unsafe-eval for React's debugging features.

options.text: CDNs cache one variant per nonce, so performance is unchanged
options.why: Each nonce is unique, so per-nonce variants would never be reused.

explanation: The CSP guide lists the trade-offs of nonces: every page is dynamically rendered, static generation and ISR are disabled, pages cannot be CDN-cached by default, and PPR is incompatible. On the plus side, Next.js attaches the nonce to its own scripts and styles automatically. In development the policy also needs `'unsafe-eval'` because React uses `eval` for debugging, which production does not need.
reference: Next.js docs: Content Security Policy

stem: A Client Component contains `const key = process.env.PAYMENTS_SECRET` (no `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefix) and renders a hint built from it. In the browser the value is `undefined`. Why do the Next.js docs still treat this as a mistake?

options.text: It is not a mistake: unprefixed variables are always undefined in Client Components
options.why: Client Components also run on the server during prerendering, where the value may exist.

options.text: Client Components also render on the server, so the HTML can carry it
options.why: They must follow browser-level security assumptions even when running on the server.

options.text: Next.js inlines every variable it finds in a Client Component at build time
options.why: Only NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are inlined into client bundles.

options.text: It causes the variable to be logged in the browser console
options.why: There is no automatic logging of environment variables.

explanation: On the initial load, Client Components run on the server to generate HTML as well as in the browser. The docs say they must follow the same security assumptions as browser code and must not access privileged data. A Client Component that reads a secret can embed something derived from it in the server-rendered HTML even though the browser bundle sees `undefined`, and the mismatch also causes hydration errors. Keep secrets in server-only modules, ideally only in the DAL.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (Passing data from server to client)

options.text: None: the cache key includes `userId`, so entries never mix
options.why: The key is correct; the problem is who chooses the userId.

options.text: It trusts a client-chosen `userId`, exposing anyone's notes
options.why: The cached getter is exported and fed an untrusted ID.

options.text: The `'use cache'` scope shares one entry across all users
options.why: Arguments are part of the cache key, so users get separate entries.

options.text: cacheTag exposes the tag name to the client, revealing user IDs
options.why: Tags are server-side cache metadata, not sent to the browser.

explanation: Caching by `userId` is fine; letting the caller choose the `userId` is not. The Cache Components authentication guide resolves the current user inside an exported getter and passes only that ID to an unexported `'use cache'` function, so no caller can ask for another user's data. A plain `'use cache'` scope cannot read `cookies()` itself, which is why the session must be read outside it and the ID passed in.
reference: Next.js docs: Authentication with Cache Components (Step 4)

stem: A sign-in page ends with `redirect(next?.startsWith('/') ? next : '/dashboard')`, where `next` comes from the query string. Which value sends the user to an attacker's site?

options.text: `next=/dashboard?x=https://evil.example`
options.why: It starts a same-origin path; the URL in the query is just data.

options.text: `next=//evil.example/login`
options.why: It starts with "/", and a URL starting with "//" is protocol-relative, so it points to another host.

options.text: `next=https://evil.example`
options.why: It does not start with "/", so the code falls back to /dashboard.

options.text: `next=/%2F%2Fevil.example`
options.why: After the leading slash this is a path on your own site, not a new host.

explanation: `startsWith('/')` is a common but incomplete open-redirect guard. A URL beginning with `//` is protocol-relative, so `//evil.example/login` resolves to another host. Browsers also treat `/\evil.example` similarly. Reject values starting with `//` or `/\`, or parse with `new URL(next, origin)` and require the result's `origin` to equal yours, then redirect to its pathname and search.
reference: OWASP: Unvalidated Redirects and Forwards Cheat Sheet

stem: An inline Server Action closes over `const apiKey = process.env.PARTNER_KEY` defined in the page component. Which statement matches the Next.js docs?

options.text: Captured variables are never sent to the client, so this is completely safe
options.why: Captured values do travel to the client and back, which is why they are encrypted.

options.text: It is encrypted in transit, but the docs say not to rely on that
options.why: Encryption is a safety net; secrets should be read inside the action instead.

options.text: The value is sent to the client in plain text inside the form
options.why: Next.js encrypts closed-over variables automatically.

options.text: Closures over environment variables throw a build error
options.why: There is no such build error; the pattern compiles.

explanation: An inline action that captures outer variables needs those values when it is invoked later, so Next.js sends them to the client and back, encrypted with a per-build private key. The docs explicitly say not to rely on encryption alone to keep sensitive values off the client. Read secrets inside the action body or in a server-only module instead of capturing them, and use closures only for non-sensitive snapshots such as a version number.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (Closures and encryption)

stem: To debug a production-only crash, a developer sets `productionBrowserSourceMaps: true` in `next.config.js` and deploys. What is the security consequence?

options.text: None: source maps are only read by browser DevTools on the developer's own machine
options.why: Next.js writes the maps next to the JS bundles and serves them to anyone who requests them.

options.text: The original client source is public, since Next.js serves the maps beside the bundles
options.why: Anyone can fetch them, including comments and the code of your Client Components.

options.text: Server Component and Server Action source is published too
options.why: The option generates browser source maps for client bundles; server-only code is not in them.

options.text: The maps are protected by the build ID, so only requests that know it can download them
options.why: The docs give no such protection: the maps are served automatically next to the JS.

explanation: Production builds turn browser source maps off by default "to prevent you leaking your source on the client". With `productionBrowserSourceMaps: true`, the maps are written next to the JavaScript files and Next.js serves them automatically, so anyone can rebuild your readable client-side code, comments included. The setting covers client bundles, not server-only code, but it still exposes business logic and makes probing easier. It also slows `next build` and uses more memory. To debug production errors, upload the maps privately to an error tracker instead of serving them publicly.
reference: Next.js docs: productionBrowserSourceMaps

stem: Behind a corporate reverse proxy, the public site is `app.example.com` but the Next.js server sees requests whose Host and X-Forwarded-Host are `internal-app.local`. Every Server Action now fails. What is the right fix?

options.text: Turn off the CSRF check, because the proxy already authenticates users
options.why: Removing the Origin check reopens CSRF; the docs offer a targeted setting instead.

options.text: List the public origin in `serverActions.allowedOrigins`
options.why: Next.js then accepts that Origin even though it differs from the Host.

options.text: Convert the forms to GET so the Origin header is not sent
options.why: Server Actions only accept POST, and GET mutations would be unsafe anyway.

options.text: Strip the Origin header at the proxy so the comparison is skipped
options.why: That weakens CSRF protection, and the check may then reject the request anyway.

explanation: Next.js protects Server Actions by comparing the request's `Origin` with the `Host` (or `X-Forwarded-Host`) and rejecting mismatches. When a reverse proxy or multi-layer setup makes the server-side host differ from the public domain, the docs recommend listing the safe origins in `serverActions.allowedOrigins`, for example `['app.example.com']` (wildcards like `'*.example.com'` are supported). Better still, configure the proxy to forward the correct `X-Forwarded-Host`.
reference: Next.js docs: serverActions (allowedOrigins)

stem: Match each response header, which you might set in `next.config.js` `headers()`, with the threat it mainly addresses.

options.text: Downgrade to plain HTTP
options.why: HSTS forces HTTPS for future visits.

options.text: Clickjacking in a hostile iframe
options.why: Controls who may frame the page.

options.text: MIME-type sniffing of uploads
options.why: Stops the browser guessing a content type.

options.text: Leaking full URLs to other sites
options.why: Limits what the Referer header reveals.

explanation: The Next.js headers docs list recommended security headers. HSTS makes browsers use HTTPS only. CSP `frame-ancestors`, which supersedes `X-Frame-Options`, prevents your pages being embedded for clickjacking. `nosniff` stops browsers treating a file as a different type than declared, for example running an uploaded file as script. `Referrer-Policy` controls how much of your URL, which may contain tokens or IDs, is sent to other origins.
reference: Next.js docs: headers (Security headers)

stem: To let users show avatars from anywhere, a team sets `images: { remotePatterns: [{ hostname: '**' }] }`. What is the main risk?

options.text: Avatars load slower, because `**` disables image caching
options.why: Wildcards affect which URLs are allowed, not caching.

options.text: It becomes an open image proxy anyone can abuse at your cost
options.why: Omitted protocol, port, pathname and search also default to `**`, which the docs advise against.

options.text: Next.js refuses to start because `**` is not valid in hostname
options.why: `**` is valid at the start of a hostname to match subdomains.

options.text: Images are served without Content-Type headers
options.why: The optimizer still sets content types; the pattern only controls allowed sources.

explanation: `remotePatterns` is an allowlist for the built-in Image Optimization API. A hostname of `**`, with protocol, port, pathname and search omitted (which also implies `**`), turns your server into a general-purpose image proxy. Attackers can then make it fetch and transform URLs you never intended, wasting compute and bandwidth and widening SSRF exposure. Pin the protocol, the exact host, a pathname prefix such as `/account123/**` and, ideally, the `search` string.
reference: Next.js docs: Image component (remotePatterns)

stem: If an image URL allowed by `remotePatterns` responds with an HTTP redirect, the Next.js image optimizer checks the redirect target against `remotePatterns` again before following it.

options.text: True
options.why: The docs say redirect targets are not re-validated against remotePatterns.

options.text: False
options.why: Redirects from allowed hosts are followed without re-checking remotePatterns.

explanation: The default loader follows up to 3 redirects when fetching remote images, and the docs note those redirects do not need to satisfy `remotePatterns`. An allowed host with an open redirect can therefore send the optimizer somewhere else. Set `images.maximumRedirects` to `0` to disable following redirects, or lower it, if your image sources do not need them. Local IP addresses stay blocked unless you set `dangerouslyAllowLocalIP`.
reference: Next.js docs: Image component (maximumRedirects, remotePatterns)

stem: A team enables `images.dangerouslyAllowSVG: true` so user-uploaded SVG logos can be optimized. Which extra configuration do the Next.js docs strongly recommend alongside it?

options.text: Set `unoptimized: true` globally so SVGs are never processed
options.why: That turns off optimization for every image, not just the risky case.

options.text: `contentDispositionType: 'attachment'` and an image CSP
options.why: Opening the image URL then downloads it, and embedded scripts cannot run.

options.text: Add the SVG host to `remotePatterns` with `search: ''`
options.why: That limits sources but does nothing about scripts inside allowed SVGs.

options.text: Set `maximumRedirects: 0` so SVGs cannot redirect
options.why: Redirects are a separate concern; the danger is script inside the SVG.

explanation: SVG supports many HTML and CSS features, including script, so serving user SVGs from your origin can enable XSS. If you enable `dangerouslyAllowSVG`, the docs strongly recommend `contentDispositionType: 'attachment'`, the default since v15, so direct visits download rather than render. They also recommend an image `contentSecurityPolicy` such as `"default-src 'self'; script-src 'none'; sandbox;"` so embedded scripts cannot execute. For known-safe static SVGs, the `unoptimized` prop is the simpler choice.
reference: Next.js docs: Image component (dangerouslyAllowSVG, contentDispositionType)

stem: With `experimental.taint: true` in next.config, a team calls `experimental_taintUniqueValue('Do not pass tokens to the client', process, user.apiToken)` in its data layer. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)

options.text: Passing `user.apiToken` to a Client Component now throws instead of leaking
options.why: React blocks tainted values at the server-client boundary.

options.text: It is an extra safety net, not a replacement for returning minimal DTOs
options.why: The docs warn against relying on taint as the only protection.

options.text: It encrypts the token so it can be sent to the client safely
options.why: Taint does not encrypt anything; it refuses to serialize the value.

options.text: It also stops the token from being logged or sent to third-party APIs
options.why: Taint only guards the React server-to-client boundary.

options.text: It works on the stable React channel without any configuration
options.why: The option enables React's experimental channel for the app directory.

explanation: The taint APIs let you mark objects (`experimental_taintObjectReference`) or unique values (`experimental_taintUniqueValue`) that React must refuse to pass to Client Components. A leak then becomes a thrown error. Enabling `experimental.taint` also switches the app directory to React's experimental channel and taints `process.env` so it cannot be passed whole to a Client Component. The docs are explicit that this is defensive layering: still filter data in the DAL.
reference: Next.js docs: taint; Data Security (Tainting)

stem: A Route Handler `GET /api/me` returns the signed-in user's profile with `Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=60` to reduce load. Shortly after deploying, users report seeing someone else's name. What happened?

options.text: Next.js deduplicated the `fetch` calls across users with React cache
options.why: React cache is scoped to a single request, not shared across users.

options.text: A CDN cached one user's response and served it to others
options.why: `public, s-maxage` tells shared caches to store and reuse the response.

options.text: The session cookie was cached in the browser and sent to the wrong user
options.why: Browsers do not share cookies between users.

options.text: Route Handlers are static by default, so it was built once at deploy time
options.why: Reading the request cookies makes this handler dynamic.

explanation: `public` with `s-maxage` explicitly allows shared caches (CDNs and proxies) to store a response and serve it to other clients. For personalized data, use `Cache-Control: private, no-store`, or at least `private`, so only the user's own browser may cache it. Do not mark responses that depend on cookies as publicly cacheable. Within Next.js, keep per-user data out of shared server caches too: pass a resolved user ID into `'use cache'`, or use `'use cache: private'`.
reference: MDN: Cache-Control; Next.js docs: Authentication with Cache Components

stem: Auth is checked only in `app/dashboard/layout.tsx`. `app/dashboard/billing/page.tsx` fetches invoices with no check. A user loads `/dashboard`, their session is revoked server-side, and then they click a `<Link>` to `/dashboard/billing`. What happens?

options.text: The layout re-runs its check during the navigation and redirects to /login
options.why: Shared layouts are preserved during client navigation, so the check is not repeated.

options.text: The billing page renders and returns invoices, because only the new segment renders
options.why: Partial rendering skips the unchanged layout and its check.

options.text: The client router cache refuses to navigate because the session cookie changed
options.why: The router cache does not inspect or validate auth cookies.

options.text: Proxy blocks it, because Proxy reruns every layout check on navigation
options.why: Proxy runs its own code, not your layout code, and only if one exists and matches.

explanation: On client navigation the App Router renders only the segments that change, so `layout.tsx` and its `redirect` are not executed again. The billing page's data fetch runs without any check and the invoices are sent. The guide recommends checks close to the data: `getInvoices()` in the DAL should call `verifySession()`, so every caller is protected whichever layout happens to render.
reference: Next.js docs: Authentication (Layouts and auth checks)

stem: A layout renders a parallel route slot only for admins: `{session.isAdmin ? admin : null}`, where `admin` comes from `@admin/page.tsx`, which queries all users' emails. What does a non-admin's request return?

options.text: No admin data, because the slot is never rendered when the layout returns null for it
options.why: The router renders slots independently of whether the layout places them.

options.text: The slot still renders, so its output can still end up in the RSC payload
options.why: Hiding a slot in the layout does not stop it from running.

options.text: A 403 error, because parallel routes enforce the parent layout's conditions
options.why: Parallel routes have no built-in authorization tied to layout logic.

options.text: Only the slot's loading.tsx fallback, because hidden slots stay suspended
options.why: A hidden slot is not kept suspended; it is rendered by the router.

explanation: The authentication guide warns that route segments and parallel route slots are rendered by the router, so a layout that hides or swaps them does not stop them from running or from appearing in the RSC payload. Conditional rendering is presentation, not access control. The `@admin` page (or the DAL function it calls) must verify the admin role itself and return nothing sensitive otherwise.
reference: Next.js docs: Authentication (Layouts and auth checks)

stem: In March 2025, CVE-2025-29927 let crafted requests skip Next.js middleware (now called Proxy) entirely on affected self-hosted versions. Which two lessons follow from Next.js's own authorization guidance? (Choose two.)

options.text: Apps that also checked auth in their Data Access Layer kept their data protected
options.why: Skipping middleware only skipped the optimistic redirect.

options.text: Proxy-only auth is a single point of failure for every protected route
options.why: The docs say Proxy should not be the only line of defense.

options.text: Moving auth from Proxy into the root layout would have fully prevented the issue
options.why: Layout checks have their own gaps, such as partial rendering on navigation.

options.text: The fix is to run database session checks in Proxy instead of cookie checks
options.why: Proxy runs on every route and prefetch; the docs advise cookie-only checks there.

options.text: Server Actions were safe because they bypass Proxy by design
options.why: Actions are POSTs to page routes; their safety comes from their own checks.

explanation: The incident is a textbook case for defense in depth. Teams that used middleware only for optimistic redirects, as the docs recommend, and re-verified the session in the DAL, pages, actions and Route Handlers, lost only a redirect when middleware was skipped. Teams relying on middleware alone exposed protected pages and APIs. Beyond upgrading promptly, keep the secure check next to the data.
reference: Next.js docs: Authentication (Optimistic checks with Proxy); Next.js security advisory CVE-2025-29927

options.text: Helper 1, because React cache shares results across all requests
options.why: React cache memoizes within a single server request (render pass).

options.text: Helper 2, because a module-level variable persists across requests
options.why: The first user to arrive is cached for everyone served by that process.

options.text: Both, because any memoization of the user is unsafe
options.why: Per-request memoization with React cache is the documented pattern.

options.text: Neither, because cookies() makes every function call request-scoped
options.why: cookies() is request-scoped, but a module variable is not.

explanation: The DAL examples wrap `verifySession` and `getCurrentUser` in React's `cache`, which memoizes for the duration of one server request, so many components can share the lookup safely. A module-level variable lives as long as the server process and is shared by every concurrent request. Whoever arrives first is returned to everyone after them, a classic cross-user leak that only shows up under real traffic.
reference: Next.js docs: Authentication (Creating a Data Access Layer); react.dev: cache

stem: You are auditing a Next.js 16 codebase for data-security issues. Which three items are on the Next.js docs' audit checklist? (Choose three.)

options.text: Are database packages or `process.env` imported outside the Data Access Layer?
options.why: Secrets and DB access should be confined to the DAL.

options.text: Do `'use client'` components declare props broader than they render?
options.why: Broad prop types invite passing whole private objects.

options.text: Do `'use server'` actions re-authorize, check ownership and limit return values?
options.why: Actions are public entry points and must defend themselves.

options.text: Is every page statically generated to shrink the attack surface?
options.why: Rendering mode is not a security control on that checklist.

options.text: Is the number of Client Components below a safe threshold?
options.why: There is no component-count rule; what matters is what they receive.

explanation: The Data Security guide's audit list covers several areas. Is there an isolated DAL, with database packages and environment variables not imported outside it? Do `"use client"` props expect private data, or are their types overly broad? Do `"use server"` actions validate arguments, re-authorize, check ownership and constrain return values? Are dynamic `[param]` inputs validated? And because `proxy.ts` and `route.ts` are powerful, they deserve traditional security review and penetration testing.
reference: Next.js docs: Data Security (Auditing)

stem: A compliance rule says personalized account data must never be stored in any server-side cache shared across requests. With Cache Components enabled, you still want to avoid repeated session reads within a request and allow client-side reuse. Which directive fits?

options.text: `'use cache'`, passing the userId in as an argument
options.why: Its result is stored on the server keyed by the arguments, which the rule forbids.

options.text: `'use cache: remote'` with a short `cacheLife`
options.why: Remote caching stores results in a server-side cache handler.

options.text: `'use cache: private'`, which may read `cookies()`
options.why: Results are kept in the browser only and never stored in a server cache across requests.

options.text: No directive: wrap the function in `unstable_cache` with a user tag
options.why: unstable_cache also persists results on the server.

explanation: `'use cache: private'` is designed for request-specific data. It can call `cookies()`, `headers()` and read `searchParams`, which plain `'use cache'` and `'use cache: remote'` cannot. Its results are not stored in a server cache across production requests. Matching calls within one request can reuse the result, and the client router can keep the output in browser memory for the configured stale time. `connection()` is still prohibited inside it.
reference: Next.js docs: use cache: private; Authentication with Cache Components

stem: Put the steps of a secure `archiveProject(formData)` Server Action in the order they should run.

options.text: Parse and validate the FormData with a schema such as zod
options.why: Validate

options.text: Verify the session and identify the caller
options.why: Authenticate

options.text: Load the project by ID and check the caller may archive it
options.why: Authorize

options.text: Archive the project in the database
options.why: Mutate

options.text: Revalidate the affected tags or paths
options.why: Revalidate

options.text: Return a minimal result such as `{ ok: true }`
options.why: Respond

explanation: Validate input first, returning early on malformed requests without touching the auth provider or database, as the authentication guide suggests. Then authenticate, then authorize against the specific resource, which prevents IDOR. Only then mutate, then revalidate so the UI shows fresh data, and finally return a small, safe value, because action return values are serialized to the client. Authenticating before validating is also acceptable; what matters is that authorization happens before the mutation and that no raw records are returned.
reference: Next.js docs: Server Actions (Security); Data Security

stem: A Route Handler implements link previews: `const res = await fetch(searchParams.get('url')!)`. It runs inside your cloud VPC. Which three changes meaningfully reduce the server-side request forgery (SSRF) risk? (Choose three.)

options.text: Allow only `https:` URLs whose host is on an allowlist
options.why: An allowlist is far stronger than trying to enumerate bad hosts.

options.text: Resolve the hostname and reject private, loopback and link-local IPs
options.why: This blocks targets like 127.0.0.1, 10.0.0.0/8 and 169.254.169.254 metadata.

options.text: Use `redirect: 'manual'` and re-check any redirect target
options.why: An allowed host could otherwise redirect the fetch to an internal address.

options.text: Reject URLs whose text contains "localhost" or "127.0.0.1"
options.why: Encodings such as 127.1, decimal IPs, IPv6 or DNS names bypass string checks.

options.text: Require the user to be signed in before fetching
options.why: Authentication limits who can attack, not what the server can be made to reach.

explanation: SSRF turns your server into a proxy into your private network, for example cloud metadata at `169.254.169.254`. Effective defenses validate the destination after parsing and resolution: an allowlist of schemes and hosts, rejecting private, loopback and link-local ranges for the resolved IP, which also guards against DNS tricks, and refusing to follow redirects blindly. String blocklists are easy to bypass. Next.js applies similar protections in its own image optimizer, which blocks local IPs unless `dangerouslyAllowLocalIP` is set.
reference: OWASP: SSRF Prevention Cheat Sheet; Next.js docs: Image component (dangerouslyAllowLocalIP)

stem: A multi-tenant app's `proxy.ts` derives the tenant from the subdomain and sets an `x-tenant-id` request header. Its matcher excludes `/api`. Route Handlers under `/api` trust `request.headers.get('x-tenant-id')`. What is the flaw?

options.text: None: request headers set in Proxy cannot be forged by clients
options.why: Headers Proxy sets are trustworthy only on requests Proxy actually handles.

options.text: For `/api` requests Proxy never runs, so a client-sent x-tenant-id reaches the handler untouched
options.why: Anyone can claim any tenant on the excluded routes.

options.text: Route Handlers cannot read headers that Proxy sets
options.why: Handlers can read forwarded request headers; that is not the issue.

options.text: Subdomains cannot be read in Proxy, so the tenant is always empty
options.why: Proxy can read the request URL and Host header.

explanation: A header is trustworthy only if your own code sets or overwrites it on every request path that reads it. Here the matcher skips `/api`, so a client can send `x-tenant-id: victim` directly to those handlers. Derive tenant identity on the server where it is used, from the authenticated session or the Host, ideally in the DAL. If you use a forwarded header, make sure Proxy strips or overwrites it for every route that consumes it.
reference: Next.js docs: Proxy (matcher); Data Security (Validating client input)

stem: A list renders `<form action={archiveItem.bind(null, item.id)}>` only for items the user owns. `archiveItem(id: string)` checks that the user is signed in, then archives the item. Is this safe?

options.text: Yes: bound arguments are fixed on the server and cannot be changed by the client
options.why: The ID is still supplied by the browser when the action is invoked.

options.text: No: a caller can invoke the action with any ID, so it must check ownership itself
options.why: Rendering forms only for owned items is a UI choice, not authorization.

options.text: Yes, as long as the page that renders the forms checks the session
options.why: Page-level checks do not extend to the action's own request.

options.text: No: `.bind` is not supported for Server Actions, so the ID will be undefined
options.why: Binding arguments to Server Actions is a supported pattern.

explanation: However an argument reaches a Server Action, through `.bind`, FormData or a direct call, it arrives in a request the client controls. Next.js tells you to treat action arguments as untrusted and to check authorization for the specific resource. `archiveItem` should load the item and confirm the caller owns it (or has the right role) before changing it. Deciding which forms to render does nothing to stop a direct POST with a different ID.
reference: Next.js docs: Server Actions (Security); Data Security

stem: Next.js's built-in CSRF protection for Server Actions compares the request's `Origin` header with which header, or `X-Forwarded-Host` when present? Type the header name.
explanation: For every Server Action request, Next.js compares the `Origin` header with the `Host` header, or with `X-Forwarded-Host` when a proxy sets it, and rejects mismatches. Combined with POST-only invocation and SameSite cookies, this blocks cross-site form submissions. Setups where the public origin legitimately differs from the host need `serverActions.allowedOrigins`.
reference: Next.js docs: Server Actions (Security)

stem: An auth library caches session data in a signed cookie for 5 minutes, so most requests skip the database. An admin bans a user at 12:00:00. The banned user, mid-session, calls a "transfer funds" Server Action at 12:01:00, and the action calls the same cookie-cached `getSession()`. What happens, and what is the fix?

options.text: The transfer is blocked, because banning deletes the cookie in the user's browser
options.why: The server cannot delete a cookie in a browser that is not making a request to it.

options.text: It can succeed until the cache expires; sensitive actions should check the database
options.why: Bypassing the cookie cache there makes revocation take effect at once.

options.text: It is blocked, because signed cookies are re-verified against the database on each request
options.why: Signing proves the cookie is untampered, not that the session is still valid.

options.text: It succeeds forever, because signed sessions can never be revoked
options.why: Database sessions can be revoked; the cached copy only delays it.

explanation: Caching session data in a signed cookie is an optimistic, stateless check: the signature proves the server issued it, but nothing re-checks the database until the cache lifetime ends, so a ban or logout elsewhere is not seen for up to that long. The Next.js guide separates optimistic checks, suited to UI and redirects, from secure checks against database session data before sensitive operations. For high-risk actions, verify against the source of truth. Many libraries expose a way to skip the cookie cache, such as Better Auth's `disableCookieCache` option.
reference: Next.js docs: Authentication (Optimistic vs secure checks); Better Auth docs: Session management
